lessons.title: Understanding the Speaking Test
lessons.bite: A live interview with a real examiner, about 11-14 minutes, in three parts. The examiner isn't your opponent -- they want you to speak, because they can't score silence.
lessons.detail_md:
### The three parts
- **Part 1** (4-5 min): short personal questions -- home, work, hobbies. A warm-up, should feel like easy small talk.
- **Part 2** (3-4 min): a task card, 1 minute to prepare, then you speak alone for 1-2 minutes. The only part where you speak at length alone.
- **Part 3** (4-5 min): broader, abstract discussion connected to Part 2's topic. The most demanding part -- it asks you to think, not just describe.

### The four criteria
**Fluency and Coherence** -- smooth flow, staying on track (not about speed). **Lexical Resource** -- range and precision, paraphrasing around unknown words. **Grammatical Range and Accuracy.** **Pronunciation** -- intelligibility, not a British/American accent.

### What the examiner is NOT judging
Your opinions (no right or wrong answers). Your knowledge (it's a language test). Your accent (any clear accent is fine). Whether your stories are true (you may invent freely).

### Tutor insider tip
The examiner cannot give marks for silence, so your first duty is simply to keep speaking. A candidate who talks naturally, even with small mistakes, always outscores one who says little for fear of being wrong.

> পরীক্ষক নীরবতায় নম্বর দিতে পারেন না -- তাই প্রথম কাজ কথা বলে যাওয়া। ছোট ভুল করলেও স্বাভাবিকভাবে কথা বলা প্রার্থী ভয়ে চুপ থাকা প্রার্থীর চেয়ে বেশি নম্বর পায়।

lessons.title: The Speaking Mindset
lessons.bite: Fluency is not speed. Treat the test as a conversation, not a performance -- speak at a comfortable pace, recover from mistakes by continuing, and extend answers naturally.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Most candidates treat Speaking as an exam requiring correct, impressive answers. That mindset makes them stiff, slow, and afraid.

### The reframe
You are not reciting; you are talking, to an interested stranger.

### Fluency is not speed
Speaking fast is not the same as speaking fluently. Fluency is smooth, connected flow -- you can be perfectly fluent at a moderate pace. Speaking too fast usually causes more errors and unclear pronunciation.

### Thinking while speaking
You don't need the perfect answer fully formed before you open your mouth. Start with a general response, then develop it as you go.

### Recovering from mistakes
The damage isn't the error -- it's stopping, apologising, and restarting, which breaks the fluency that's actually being scored. When you slip, keep going.

### Extending answers
Don't give bare one-word answers, which starve the examiner of language to assess. Don't over-talk either. The target: enough to show range, then a natural stop.

### Tutor insider tip
"Do you enjoy cooking?" A beginner says "Yes." An expert says: "Yes, I really enjoy it, especially at weekends when I have time to try new recipes... though I have to admit I'm much better at desserts than main meals." Answered, with a reason, a detail, a touch of personality, then a natural stop.

> দ্রুত বলা মানেই সাবলীল নয়। স্বাভাবিক গতিতে কথা বলুন, ভুল হলে থেমে ক্ষমা না চেয়ে চালিয়ে যান।

lessons.title: Speaking Part 1: Answer, Reason, Detail
lessons.bite: Two to four sentences is the sweet spot for Part 1. Answer directly, say why briefly, add a detail -- but don't let it become a robotic formula.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** One word is too little; a one-minute monologue is too much and out of place here.

### The core framework
**Answer** -- respond directly first. **Reason** -- say why, briefly. **Detail** -- add an example or personal colour.

*Example ("Do you prefer tea or coffee?"):* "I much prefer coffee, actually. (Answer.) It's mainly the caffeine, since I need it to wake up properly. (Reason.) I usually have a strong cup before work, and I've become a bit fussy about how it's made. (Detail.)"

### Do not sound formulaic
The framework is training wheels, not a rigid template to repeat identically. Vary how you start -- sometimes lead with a preference or contrast. As you improve, the shape becomes invisible.

### Common mistakes
One-word answers. Memorised speeches. Turning Part 1 into Part 2 (a long monologue). Answering a slightly different question than what was asked (it's fine to ask the examiner to repeat).

### Tutor insider tip
Answer the question you were actually asked, then add a little. "Do you like your job?" wants your feeling and a reason, not a two-minute career history. Match the size of your answer to the size of the question.

> Answer, Reason, Detail -- তিনটা বাক্য যথেষ্ট। প্রশ্নের আকারের সাথে উত্তরের আকার মেলান।

lessons.title: How to Extend an Answer
lessons.bite: A bare answer gives the examiner almost nothing to score. Use the extension toolkit -- reason, example, contrast, personal experience, consequence -- to add range naturally.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Learning to extend any answer naturally is perhaps the single most useful Speaking skill, applying across all three parts.

### The extension toolkit
Reason ("because," "mainly because"). Example ("for example," "like when"). Contrast ("but," "although," "on the other hand"). Personal experience ("I remember once"). Consequence ("so," "as a result"). Preference/comparison. Hypothetical/future ("I would love to," "one day I hope to").

You don't use all of them at once -- pick one or two that fit.

### The worked transformation
Bare: "Yes, I like travelling." With reason+example: "Yes, I love travelling, mainly because it lets me experience completely different ways of life. Last year, for instance, I visited a small fishing village..." Same starting point, four different natural extended answers using different tool combinations.

### How much is enough
Part 1: 2-4 sentences, one or two extension moves. Part 3: more, since those questions invite discussion. The skill is not maximum length -- it's adding enough to show range, then stopping before you ramble.

### Tutor insider tip
When stuck, silently ask "why?" or "for example?" of your own answer, and say the reply out loud. These two questions extend almost any answer naturally.

> আটকে গেলে নিজেকে জিজ্ঞাসা করুন "কেন?" বা "উদাহরণ?" -- এই দুটো প্রশ্নই প্রায় যেকোনো উত্তর স্বাভাবিকভাবে বাড়িয়ে দেয়।

lessons.title: Part 2 Cue Cards: The Universal System
lessons.bite: A five-part skeleton for any cue card: introduce, facts, story, feelings and reasons, reflection. The 'explain' prompt is the most important line on the card -- spend most of your minute preparing it.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Many candidates rush the facts and neglect the "explain" prompt -- do the opposite; that's where the marks live.

### Using the one minute
Don't write sentences -- you won't have time, and reading them aloud sounds unnatural. Jot keywords only. You're preparing a story to tell, not a script to read.

### The five-part skeleton
1. **Introduce** -- "I'd like to tell you about..."
2. **The facts** -- who, what, where, when.
3. **The story or description** -- what happened, in order, or vivid detail.
4. **Feelings and reasons** -- answer the "explain" prompt. Spend real time here.
5. **Reflection or result** -- what it means to you now.

### Creating a story
Shape it chronologically (before/during/after) or descriptively (senses and specifics). Tenses shift naturally: past for events, present for how you feel now.

### Adapt, do not memorise
You cannot memorise an answer for every possible card. Internalise the system and practise applying it to random cards until automatic.

### Tutor insider tip
Spend most of your minute preparing the "explain" prompt, not the facts. Anyone can say where and when; the marks are in why and how you felt.

> এক মিনিটের বেশিরভাগ সময় "explain" অংশের জন্য দিন -- কোথায়-কখন যে কেউ বলতে পারে, নম্বর থাকে কেন আর কেমন লেগেছিল তাতে।

lessons.title: What If I Don't Know the Topic?
lessons.bite: Invent plausibly, adapt a real memory, or generalise then commit. The examiner is testing your English, not fact-checking your life -- you are allowed to invent.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Sometimes you get a card with no real experience to draw on. This is not a problem.

### Three strategies
1. **Invent plausibly.** Build a believable example from general knowledge -- a famous building seen in photos, described as if visited.
2. **Adapt a real memory.** Bend a real experience to fit the card.
3. **Generalise, then commit.** "I haven't travelled abroad much, but if I had to choose a memorable trip, it would be..." Then treat that as your answer.

### What not to do
Don't say "I don't know" and stop. Don't fall silent. Don't announce you're making it up. Simply construct your answer naturally and speak as though it's yours.

### Tutor insider tip
A vivid, well-told imaginary answer scores far higher than an honest "I can't think of one." The examiner will never know, and it is not their concern.

> "জানি না" বলে থেমে যাবেন না। আপনি কল্পনা করতে পারেন -- এটা অনুমোদিত এবং সৎ "ভাবতে পারছি না"-এর চেয়ে অনেক বেশি নম্বর পায়।

lessons.title: How to Keep Talking: The Rescue System
lessons.bite: When your mind runs dry mid-answer, run through eight moves: add detail, explain, example, compare, reflect, feelings, consequence, speculate. Real content, never empty filler.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** This happens to everyone -- Part 2 or deep in Part 3, mind empties with time still to fill.

### The rescue moves
Add detail. Explain (why/how). Give an example. Compare. Reflect. Feelings. Consequence. Speculate.

You don't use all eight -- reach for whichever fits, and it restarts your flow.

### Worked rescue
Dry answer: "My favourite gadget is my phone. I use it all the time." Apply moves: *Explain* -- "I rely on it because it does almost everything." *Example* -- "I planned my whole last holiday on it." *Compare* -- "A few years ago I needed a separate camera, map, and diary." *Reflect* -- "It worries me how dependent I've become." Four moves turned two dead sentences into a full answer.

### Do not fill with empty filler
Avoid strings of "um, yeah, so, I don't know" -- these lower Fluency. The rescue moves give you something genuine to say.

### Tutor insider tip
Memorise the rescue moves as a short mental list: explain, example, compare, feel, reflect. When you freeze, silently walk the list and pick one. You are never truly stuck -- you have simply not asked yourself the next question yet.

> আটকে গেলে মনে করুন: explain, example, compare, feel, reflect. একটা বেছে নিন -- খালি "um, uh" দিয়ে সময় নষ্ট করবেন না।

lessons.title: Speaking Part 3: The Framework
lessons.bite: Part 3 asks for opinions, analysis, and speculation about society and ideas, not personal facts. Develop every answer: Answer, Explain, Example, Consequence or Contrast.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** This is the part that most tests your Fluency and Coherence -- you must organise a genuine argument on the spot.

### The question types
Opinion ("Do you think...?"). Cause ("Why do people...?"). Effect. Comparison. Change over time. Prediction (use "might," "could," "is likely to"). Advantages/disadvantages or problem/solution.

### The core framework
**Answer** -- your response directly. **Explain** -- the reasoning. **Example** -- a specific instance. **Consequence or Contrast** -- the result, or the other side.

### Language that adds range and buys time
"I suppose," "generally speaking," "it depends," "some might argue," "on balance." These signal sophistication AND give thinking space.

### Handling "it depends"
A legitimate, sophisticated answer -- but only if you then explain the conditions: "It depends on the age group. For younger people... whereas for older people..."

### Tutor insider tip
In Part 3, always say why. An answer that gives an opinion and then explains and illustrates it scores far higher than a longer answer that just asserts several opinions. One well-developed reason beats three bare ones.

> Part 3-এ সবসময় কারণ বলুন -- একটা ভালোভাবে ব্যাখ্যা করা মত কয়েকটা শুধু বলে যাওয়া মতের চেয়ে বেশি নম্বর পায়।

lessons.title: Thinking Time: Buying a Natural Pause
lessons.bite: A brief pause is fine; six seconds of silence is not. Use natural openers, reformulate the question, or hedge -- these are real spoken behaviours, not stalling.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Fluent speakers of every language buy thinking time constantly, with natural moves you can learn.

### How to buy time naturally
- **A brief pause.** One second is fine; six is not.
- **A general opener.** "That's an interesting question." "I've never really thought about that, but..."
- **Reformulate the question.** "So, whether technology has made us less social... I'd say..." -- shows understanding too.
- **Natural fillers, sparingly.** "Well," "I suppose," "to be honest" -- used constantly, they become a tic.
- **Start general, then narrow.** "There are probably several reasons for that. The main one, I think, is..."
- **Hedge as thinking space.** "It's hard to say, but generally..."

### The balance: natural, not stalling
One brief opener and a short pause sound thoughtful. A five-second "ummmm," or stacking "well, you know, I mean, actually" sounds like stalling and lowers Fluency.

### Tutor insider tip
Have two or three natural openers ready and let them become automatic. They are not memorised answers, so they aren't penalised -- they're the natural connective tissue of speech.

> "That's an interesting question" জাতীয় opener প্রস্তুত রাখুন -- এগুলো মুখস্থ উত্তর নয়, penalise হয় না, আর মস্তিষ্ককে সময় দেয়।

lessons.title: Recovery Strategies
lessons.bite: Recovery beats perfection. A small mistake, smoothly passed over, costs almost nothing -- the same mistake followed by a full stop and apology costs your Fluency.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** What separates a high band from a low one is not the absence of slips -- it's how smoothly you carry on after them.

### What to do in each situation
- **Grammar mistake:** usually just carry on. A quick natural self-correction is fine ("she go, sorry, she goes"), but don't obsess.
- **Wrong word:** correct briefly and naturally, then continue.
- **Forgotten word:** don't freeze -- paraphrase around it ("the, you know, the machine you use to make coffee"). This actively demonstrates Lexical Resource.
- **Misunderstood question:** ask politely for repetition or clarification -- far better than confidently answering the wrong question.
- **Lost your train of thought:** "Anyway, my main point is..." Don't panic and restart the whole answer.
- **Spoke too much/too little:** interruption isn't a sign you did badly; too little is fixed with the extension toolkit.

### Tutor insider tip
Do not apologise for small mistakes. Stopping to say "sorry, sorry" draws the examiner's attention to an error they might have barely noticed, and breaks fluency far more than the error did.

> ছোট ভুলের জন্য বারবার sorry বলবেন না -- এটা ভুলের চেয়ে বেশি fluency নষ্ট করে। সহজ হলে ঠিক করুন, নাহলে চালিয়ে যান।

lessons.title: Pronunciation Strategy
lessons.bite: Pronunciation is scored on intelligibility, not accent. If you fix only one thing, fix monotone -- flat delivery is what most damages an otherwise good speaker.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** You do NOT need a British or American accent. A clear accent of any origin scores well.

### The features worth working on
Clarity (don't swallow endings). Word stress (comFORTable, phoTOGraphy). Sentence stress (stress content words, not every word). Rhythm. **Intonation** -- let your voice rise and fall. Pausing at natural thought-group boundaries.

### The biggest single win: avoid monotone
A monotone voice makes even good English sound dull and can obscure meaning, since English carries information in its intonation. This is the single biggest win available.

### The speed connection
Slowing slightly improves clarity -- rushed speech blurs sounds and endings.

### How to practise
Read aloud and record yourself. Listen for clarity, stress, and flatness -- not individual sounds you can't easily change.

### Tutor insider tip
Don't waste effort erasing your accent -- it isn't assessed. A candidate with a strong regional accent who speaks clearly, stresses the right words, and uses lively intonation will outscore a "neutral" accent candidate who mumbles in a monotone.

> একঘেয়ে (monotone) কণ্ঠস্বরই সবচেয়ে বড় সমস্যা -- accent মুছার চেষ্টা না করে স্পষ্টতা আর প্রাণবন্ত ওঠানামায় মনোযোগ দিন।

lessons.title: Memorisation Traps: Why Memorised Answers Hurt
lessons.bite: Examiners are trained to detect recited speech -- a giveaway rhythm, unnaturally polished vocabulary, stories forced onto the wrong cards. Prepare flexible frameworks, not scripts.
lessons.detail_md:
**Why it matters:** Memorised answers usually lower your score, for several concrete reasons.

### Why it hurts
Examiners detect it (giveaway rhythm, upward glance of recall). It rarely fits the exact question asked. Vocabulary sounds forced. Over-prepared stories get forced onto the wrong cards, and the mismatch is obvious. Delivery turns robotic, lacking natural hesitations and warmth.

### What to do instead: prepare flexibly
- Prepare ideas and vocabulary for common topics, not scripts.
- Practise the frameworks (Answer-Reason-Detail, the cue card system, Answer-Explain-Example-Consequence) until automatic -- these are flexible tools, not memorised text.
- Build a bank of personal examples you can adapt.
- Practise speaking spontaneously on random questions.

### Tutor insider tip
A natural, simple answer is almost always stronger than an impressive memorised one. The examiner would rather hear you think, hesitate slightly, and build a real answer than hear a flawless speech that clearly isn't yours.

> মুখস্থ উত্তর পরীক্ষক সহজেই ধরে ফেলেন। স্ক্রিপ্ট নয়, নমনীয় কাঠামো (framework) অনুশীলন করুন যাতে তা স্বয়ংক্রিয় হয়ে যায়।

lessons.title: Speaking Insider Tips
lessons.bite: Answer the actual question. Don't turn Part 1 into a speech. Don't stop after one sentence. Don't restart every sentence. Keep talking -- the examiner can't score silence.
lessons.detail_md:
These are honest observations from watching hundreds of candidates succeed and stumble.

### The habits that separate high scorers
- **Answer the actual question**, not a nearby topic you prepared.
- **Don't turn Part 1 into a speech** -- 2-4 sentences, matched to the question's size.
- **Don't stop after one sentence** -- extend with a reason or example.
- **Don't panic over small mistakes** -- keep the flow going.
- **Don't restart every sentence** ("I think that, no, what I mean is...") -- commit and finish, even imperfectly.
- **Don't force idioms** -- a forced one sounds worse than plain speech.
- **Don't speak unnaturally slowly or fast** -- aim for a comfortable conversational pace.
- **Don't memorise entire cue-card answers** -- prepare flexible frameworks instead.
- **In Part 3, always say why.**
- **Treat it as a conversation** -- engage, react, let personality show.
- **Remember there are no wrong opinions or stories.**
- **Keep talking** -- the examiner cannot score silence.
- **Ask for repetition if unsure** -- far better than confidently answering the wrong question.

### Tutor insider tip
If you internalise only one thing from this module, make it this: relax and talk. Almost every Speaking problem comes from fear, not weak English.

> এই মডিউল থেকে একটাই কথা মনে রাখুন: শান্ত থাকুন আর কথা বলুন। বেশিরভাগ সমস্যা ভয় থেকে আসে, দুর্বল ইংরেজি থেকে নয়।

lessons.title: Module 4 Wrap-Up: Speaking in One Breath
lessons.bite: Treat it as a real conversation. Extend Part 1 answers, build Part 2 stories around the 'why', reason through Part 3, buy time naturally, and never memorise whole answers.
lessons.detail_md:
Compressed to its core, Speaking is this:

Treat the test as a real conversation, because that is what it is. In Part 1, answer naturally and extend a little with Answer, Reason, Detail. In Part 2, use your minute for keyword notes and build a story with the universal system, spending most of your effort on the "why" and the feelings. In Part 3, answer, explain, illustrate, and add the other side, always giving your reasoning.

When you need a moment, buy it like a fluent speaker, with a short pause and a natural opener, not a pile of fillers. When you slip, keep going. When you forget a word, talk around it. Speak clearly and with lively intonation, at a comfortable pace, in your own accent. **And never memorise whole answers**, because a natural, thinking speaker always beats a reciting one.

### Tutor insider tip
That is the whole module -- not "speak well," but a precise set of habits for answering, extending, recovering, and staying calm, that you can now run in any interview. When you can do it without thinking, the examiner stops being frightening and becomes what they always were: a person having a conversation with you.

> এটাকে সত্যিকারের কথোপকথন হিসেবে দেখুন। Answer-Reason-Detail দিয়ে বাড়ান, কারণ সবসময় ব্যাখ্যা করুন, স্বাভাবিকভাবে সময় নিন, আর কখনো পুরো উত্তর মুখস্থ করবেন না।
